UPDATED 16:41 EDT / OCTOBER 02 2026
CrowdStrike and CoreWeave bring AI security to machine speed
by Victoria Gayton
AI-native cybersecurity requires defenses that can keep pace with attackers while protecting infrastructure that never stops running. That challenge is bringing security expertise and specialized computing closer together, with automation embedded throughout the systems enterprises use to train and run models.
CrowdStrike's fastest observed eCrime attacker breakout time in 2025 was 27 seconds, underscoring the urgency of faster response, according to Bartley Richardson (pictured, left), chief of AI at CrowdStrike Holdings Inc. Meeting that challenge requires computing capacity for both training and inference.
"You can't have humans combat this alone," he said. "You need machine-speed defense, and that relies on critical infrastructure."
Richardson and Jim Higgins (right), chief information security officer of CoreWeave Inc., spoke with theCUBE Research's Dave Vellante and John Furrier at the Fully Connected event , during an exclusive broadcast on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media's livestreaming studio. They discussed machine-speed defense, infrastructure-level security and operational trust. (* Disclosure below.)
Cyber models turn attacks into training data
The partnership combines CrowdStrike's security data and adversary expertise with CoreWeave's infrastructure capabilities. CoreWeave supplies training and inference capacity for SafeMind and serves as a design partner for CrowdStrike's Cyber Superintelligence Lab , according to the company.
"The name of the game ... is adversarial co-evolution, which is a fancy way of saying, 'We train and we steer the best offensive capabilities to attack, to find ways around defensive operations,'" Richardson said. "But then, we train these defensive models on large-scale infrastructure to learn from those attacks."
CoreWeave must strengthen security while keeping its production systems running. That requires integrating protective measures into ongoing operations, according to Higgins.
"That's what I refer to as the aikido of the security problem," he said. "Anything that I can do to affect security while the machine is running and use its own energy to promote the security needs is exactly what I do. Using AI to support and scan my code is incredibly important, but also to be in the [continuous integration and continuous delivery] pipeline to use automation to fix misconfigurations."
AI-native cybersecurity still starts with the basics
Attackers work within budgets and time limits, making the easiest route into an environment an attractive target. Combining several ordinary weaknesses can give them that opening, according to Higgins.
"When you say something is secure, test it and test it often to be sure, but also do the basics," he said. "Patch your stuff and continually test and monitor for those issues."
CrowdStrike is investing in automation to support continuous security operations. Those capabilities must earn the confidence of both CoreWeave and its customers, according to Richardson.
"People ask, 'When do we get to the end of AI?' And I say, 'Never,'" he said. "And then I tell them, 'It's because it's AI until you trust it. Then you start to think of it as automation.' As we make our investment into AI that's always on, what's so important for us is how trust is built into the system."

UPDATED 07:26 EDT / OCTOBER 02 2026
Enterprise storage becomes AI memory as privately run models close in on the frontier
by Ryan Stevens
As open-weight models close in on the performance of proprietary frontier systems, enterprises are gaining a credible way to run generative AI on hardware they own. That shift puts the data already sitting in corporate storage at the center of the private AI conversation.
Many organizations are now moving AI out of pilot projects and into production built on intelligent data infrastructure . The past two years went largely into getting sprawling data estates ready for AI, which is why productivity gains are now landing across industries, according to Ashish Dhawan (pictured, left), senior vice president, general manager and chief revenue officer of the Cloud Business Unit at NetApp Inc.
"There's been more maturity about the usage of models in private AI. You find that whether it's closed models or open-weight models, they're getting close to the frontier," Dhawan said. "That's where our AIPod Mini with Iterate can really work well."
Dhawan, Brian Sathianathan (center), co-founder and chief technology officer of Iterate Studio Inc., doing business as Iterate.ai, and Jon Nordmark (right), co-founder and chief executive officer of Iterate.ai, spoke with theCUBE's Christophe Bertrand at NetApp INSIGHT , during an exclusive interview on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media's livestreaming studio. They discussed how the companies' partnership packages private AI for enterprises and where agentic AI is producing measurable results. (* Disclosure below.)
Open-weight models move private AI closer to enterprise data
The partnership centers on the AIPod Mini, a turnkey appliance that pairs NetApp infrastructure with Iterate.ai's Generate platform . The goal is to keep the model, the hardware and the data under the customer's control rather than sending information to a third-party service, according to Sathianathan.
"AIPod Mini has attached connections to the NetApp storage, and it talks to NetApp using the ONTAP protocol that's time-tested," Sathianathan said. "Then on top of it, on top of the AIPod Mini, we are running our Generate software. That software has an LLM embedded in it, so you can run all your AI queries locally and fully privately within your four walls."
Out of the box, the system ships with more than 200 agent templates, more than 200 skills and access to more than 800 tools, according to Nordmark. In one insurance deployment, accident-report analysis that would normally take an analyst about eight hours was finished in eight minutes. Iterate.ai frames its approach as outcome-based AI, judged on business results rather than technical specifications.
"What we mean by that is it's got to produce the proper KPIs and business outcomes," Nordmark said. "Now, the technical things are kind of table stakes, but everything else is what really matters to the enterprise."
Healthcare offers a sharper example. Hospitals typically collect 80% to 85% of what they bill insurers, and Iterate.ai's forensic revenue cycle agent identified $17.4 million in denied claims for a hospital with $150 million in annual billing, according to Sathianathan. The workflow chains three agents that read payer contracts, examine incoming denials and draft resubmissions, Nordmark added. As agents take on that kind of back-end work, control over what they can access becomes critical.
"If these autonomous agents are beginning to run, what it also means is you want to have governance," Sathianathan said. "You want to have permission. That's where the NetApp platform is really powerful."
NetApp also used the event to launch Novus, a storage architecture engineered for zettabyte-scale capacity in AI factories. For the partners, the larger point is that capable open-weight models only pay off when they can reach the institutional knowledge held in enterprise storage.
"Memory plus context equals knowledge. We talk a lot about that. Memory is what makes AI work," Nordmark said. "So much of a company's memory is in storage today, and that's what NetApp's here to unleash."
